title: Nipah Virus (NiV) in Focus: Molecular Insights Into Pathogenesis, Transmission Dynamics, and Evolving Epidemiology From Malaysia to Recent Indian Outbreaks.
abstract: Since the emergence of the Nipah virus (NiV) in Malaysia in 1998, it has returned multiple times and continues to pose a significant threat to global public health. It is characterised by high mortality and fatality rates and increasing evidence of human-to-human transmission. The epidemiological pattern of NiV has shifted considerably over the past 2 decades, from transmission primarily associated with infected pigs to repeated spillover events linked to Pteropus fruit bats, contaminated food sources, and close human contact. NiV infection is marked by severe respiratory involvement, immune dysregulation, acute encephalitis and widespread endothelial damage contributing to rapid clinical deterioration and poor outcomes. The World Health Organisation classified the Nipah virus as a priority pathogen with high mortality and pandemic potential, with recognised outbreaks showing case fatalities ranging from 40% to 100%. The virus has been detected in the Indian subcontinent and is carried by fruit bats. Recent outbreaks reported in India through 2026 have further highlighted the ongoing threat posed by the virus and the challenges of outbreak containment in densely populated regions. Current advances in serological and Molecular diagnostics have improved early detection; however, therapeutic options remain limited, and no licenced vaccine is currently available for human use. Ongoing therapeutics research involving monoclonal antibodies, recombinant vaccines, and antiviral agent platforms continues to expand the prospects for future prevention and disease control. Outbreaks must be prevented by prompt diagnosis and the application of infection control measures. However, the lack of knowledge regarding the pathophysiology, clinical features, and current treatment of Nipah virus disease makes it difficult to design such trials. The current advances summarised herein strengthen the scientific foundation for improved diagnostic platforms, antiviral interventions, vaccine development, and integrated One Health surveillance approaches targeting Nipah Virus.

title: Nanobodies targeting a conserved henipavirus G glycoprotein receptor-binding region potently protect against Nipah virus infection.
abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) and Hendra virus (HeV) are highly lethal zoonotic henipaviruses with pandemic potential, yet no approved antiviral therapeutics are currently available. Here, we identified four nanobodies targeting the viral attachment glycoprotein (G) with strong neutralizing activity. All candidates potently neutralized NiV-Malaysia (NiV M ) and NiV-Bangladesh (NiV B ) in authentic virus assays, with IC 50 values in the low ng/mL range (2.50-18.3 ng/mL). 2E2 shows the most potent activity, with an IC 50 of 2.50 ng/mL. These candidates cross-neutralized HeV in pseudovirus assays at levels comparable to those against NiV, yet authentic HeV neutralization was reduced with the most potent clone reaching an IC50 of 160 ng/mL and the remaining clones showing variable potency. In Syrian hamsters challenged with 1000 LD 50 NiV M , prophylactic administration of 1C3, 2E2, or 5A3 provides complete protection. Notably, 2E2 confers superior therapeutic protection (66.7% survival) when administered 24 h post-infection. Additionally, 2E2 provides 50% prophylactic protection against lethal HeV. Alanine-scanning mutagenesis indicated that the nanobodies recognize a conserved region within the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of G, with distinct sensitivities to individual residue substitutions. Notably, 2E2 exhibited minimal sensitivity to the tested NiV G mutations and retained neutralizing activity against the m102.4 escape-associated substitutions NiV G-V507I and HeV G-D582N. These findings identify 2E2 as a candidate RBD-targeting nanobody with potent prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy against NiV and cross-neutralizing activity against HeV, warranting further evaluation as a countermeasure for NiV outbreaks.

title: A Synthetic Consensus Chiroptera IFN-β Induces IFN-I Signaling Across Diverse Bat Taxa
abstract: Bat-associated viruses consistently spill over from bats into humans and other animals. Many bat-associated viruses, including Marburg virus and Nipah virus, cause severe disease in humans but their presentation is subclinical in bats. Advancements in tools and resources to study bat innate antiviral immune responses, including the type I IFN (IFN-I) pathway, are needed to evaluate the mechanisms that underlie differential infection outcomes between reservoir bats and spillover hosts. Commercially available IFN-Is are not bat-specific, and conspecific IFN-Is are impractical to produce for the over 1,500 described bat species. Here, we design and validate a bat order-level consensus IFN (Chiroptera IFN-β) that is functional in bat cells from six diverse bat families, including representatives from both suborders. Using Jamaican fruit bat cells, we demonstrate that Chiroptera IFN-β induces an IFN-stimulated gene repertoire comparable to conspecific IFN-β. This valuable resource can accelerate the capacity of the field to study bat innate antiviral responses and illuminate differences between bats and humans.

title: DeepMolVir: Learning Virtual Virus Representations for Sequence-Aware Virus–Inhibitor Activity Prediction
abstract: Abstract The growing threat of emerging and drug-resistant viruses demands efficient approaches for predicting virus–inhibitor interactions. However, most existing computational models treat viruses as categorical identifiers and fail to capture sequence-level biological information. Here, we assembled a data set of 50,711 compound–virus activity pairs spanning 178 viral species and explored protein language models as a strategy for viral representation learning. Using embeddings generated by ESMC-600M, we introduce a virtual virus representation in which viruses are encoded as sequence-derived biological entities rather than as taxonomic labels. These viral representations are integrated with molecular features to model compound–virus interactions. In extensive 5-fold cross-validation, DeepMolVir demonstrated strong predictive performance, achieving an AUC of 0.8653 and an RMSE of 0.9480. Notably, virtual virus representations consistently outperformed conventional taxonomy-based encodings, while ablation studies highlighted viral sequence information as a key contributor to the model performance. Case studies on Nipah virus and hantaviruses further demonstrated the ability of DeepMolVir to identify candidate antiviral scaffolds and support cross-family drug repurposing. Collectively, our findings establish protein-language-model-based viral representation learning as an effective strategy for sequence-aware antiviral activity prediction and provide a foundation for computational antiviral discovery. Code and data are available at GitHub: https://github.com/Sunny-RPX/DeepMolVir.
journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
